title: 584 Years
on One GPU
en.r6: about 6 operations per parameter, per token
en.est: an estimate: the big matrix multiplies
en.x4: her slide: two factors of about 2
en.h11: MFU: the share of peak you use
en.m3: waiting on each other, and on memory
end: After Prof. Yufei Ding's CSE 291P, Lecture 4
Count the FLOPs before the GPUs.
fine: Llama Team 2024 (The Llama 3 Herd of Models); NVIDIA H100 specifications;
Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022. Lectures 4 and 5. The narration is a synthetic voice.

cap.n0: End of 2023.|In her scenario,|your job is to train a|405-billion-parameter model in four months.
cap.n0b: On one GPU, even at full speed,|it would take 584 years.|How can you know that before you start?
cap.n1: It's a scenario Prof.|Ding gives in her course, CSE 291P,|as it turns to training:|you, a huge job, and a deadline.
cap.n2: Why so huge?|Bigger models and more data give lower loss.|Those are the scaling laws, from 2020.|So the jobs only grow.
cap.n3: Before you touch a single GPU,|there is a quicker first step.
cap.n4: FLOPs are floating-point operations:|the multiplies and adds a chip does.|This model has 405 billion|parameters, the numbers it learns,|and it reads about 15 trillion tokens,|pieces of words.
cap.n5: A 2022 rule of thumb, Chinchilla,|says about 20 tokens per parameter.|Llama 3 used about 37.
cap.n6: Now the rule.|Training costs about six operations per parameter,|per token.|Where does six come from?
cap.n7: Going forward,|every weight does a multiply and an add for every token.|That's two.
cap.n8: Going backward costs twice that.|Here is why, in her words.
cap.n9: One gradient for the input, one for the weights:|how each number should change.|Two plus four makes six.
cap.n10: So multiply.|Six, times 405 billion, times 15 trillion.|That's 3.645 times ten to the 25 operations.
cap.n11: The paper itself reports 3.8 times ten to the 25:|the same rule, with its 15.6 trillion tokens.|It's an estimate.|It counts the big matrix multiplies and little else.
cap.n12: Picture that work as a mountain of ingredients,|and one GPU as one cook at one stove.
cap.n13: One H100 GPU, using 8-bit numbers called FP8,|peaks at 1,979 trillion operations a second.|That's without sparsity, a trick for skipping zeros,|and at 100 percent, all the time.
cap.n14: Divide. About 1.84 times ten to the ten seconds.|About 584 years.
cap.n15: A GPU that started in the 1440s|would just about be finishing.
cap.n16: But Llama 3 was trained on up to 16,000 H100s.|Split the mountain that many ways,|at full speed, and it's about 13 days.
cap.n17: Thirteen days. Easy? Then she asks the class.
cap.n18: Her slide hunts for the missing factor of four.|First.
cap.n19: MFU, model FLOPs utilization,|is the share of the peak you actually use.|Llama 3 kept 38 to 43 percent.|At 40 percent, it runs two and a half times slower.
cap.n20: Why not 100 percent?|Cooks wait on each other, and on memory. Her list.
cap.n21: And things break.|The paper gives no single total time.|It reports a 54-day stretch of|pre-training with 466 interruptions.|419 were unexpected,|and about 78 percent of those were hardware,|GPUs most of all.
cap.n22: Second.|Llama 3 trained in 16-bit numbers, not FP8,|and in 16-bit the H100 peaks at half its FP8 speed.|Another two times.
cap.n23: Her slide rounds both factors to two:|13 days times four, about 54 days.|With two and a half, it's nearer two months.|Either way, weeks, not centuries.
cap.n24: The lesson.|Count the FLOPs first, and the rest follows.
cap.n25: And the count says one GPU is hopeless.|Training has to be spread over thousands of them.|Next: what is inside a cluster like that.
cap.c1: I think you should be excited.|Usually like getting the resources is the first step.
cap.c4: I guess no matter what is the result,|you cannot bear with it, right?
cap.c6: Do you know what is the real time they are having there?|54 days.
cap.c10: So you do the calculation, you only use flops,|you get the final result.
cap.c11: So that's why in the forward, you have one time.|In the backward,|because you are doing the computation|for both input and weight.|So that's why you have two copies.
